text:
Gray November evening setting up here in Burlington. A leftover sprinkle is possible before 4, but the sun sets around 4:30 behind a blanket of cloud, so don't count on any color. Temperatures slide from the upper 40s into the 30s tonight, bottoming out around 39, and it stays dry for the most part.

Tomorrow starts dry, which makes it the better time for a walk or a bike ride. Showers move in around 1 and become most likely between about 4 and 9 in the evening, tapering off after midnight. Amounts are light, under a tenth of an inch. The high is near 51. One model is a good deal wetter than the forecasters, so I'd keep the umbrella handy. A few heavier showers could even toss in some graupel, which is just a brief burst of little white pellets. Tuesday night drops to around 35 with a breeze, but any snow stays up in the hills.

Wednesday dries out and runs a little cooler, in the upper 40s. After that, the late-week system is still a question mark.

A colder day, mostly cloudy with a high near 41 and a chance of a rain and snow mix, more likely after dark.
Mostly cloudy and raw with a high near 42, and about a coin flip for on and off rain and snow showers.
Looks mostly cloudy with a high near 44 and a lingering rain or snow shower possible, trending drier by evening.

AFD DISCUSSION (the forecaster's full reasoning, same regional caveat; their temps are area-wide ranges):
KEY MESSAGE 1: Multi layer stacked low pressure currently rotating over far eastern Quebec, centered near Anticosti Island, will keep our forecast area in classic dreary November weather into the late week. Clouds continue to blanket northern New York and Vermont this afternoon and tonight with scattered to isolated showers, then our next shortwave comes through Tuesday, greatly increasing probabilities of precipitation Tuesday and Tuesday night. Daytime highs in the mid 40s to mid 50s will mean this precipitation mainly falls in the form of rain during daylight hours. The cold pool aloft and some meager instability could allow for more robust showers to produce some graupel on Tuesday afternoon, along with brief moderately heavy rainfall and gusty winds. Overall winds out of the southwest will be breezy Tuesday, particularly on summits and eastern slopes of mountains. Gusts to 30 mph will be possible on the eastern slopes, with 35 to 45+ mph atop the mountain summits. A reinforcing shot of cold air Tuesday night will bring snow levels as low as 1500 ft or so, mainly along the international border and the northern Adirondacks/Greens, and this is the best chance for seeing any accumulating snow below 2000 ft, though even then, it'll be pretty minimal. Lows by Wednesday morning will fall into the mid 20s to mid 30s. During the day Wednesday, we'll be drying out under high pressure, with perhaps a lingering shower or two in morning for the Northeast Kingdom and seasonable afternoon highs in the 40s and lower 50s. Total precipitation amounts Tuesday through Wednesday will be as high as 0.10-0.30", with highest in the northern mountains and Northeast Kingdom. Total snow accumulations will likely be under an inch, limited to highest elevations. KEY MESSAGE 2: There remains high uncertainty with the late week system, but trends have continued to suggest a track shift south and east of the region with the newest round of guidance. A broad closed upper low will gradually shift southeast Thursday into Friday with a pair of shortwaves digging well into the Mid-Atlantic. As these shortwaves interact with the parent upper low, the associated long wave will become negatively tilted amplifying the flow pattern along the east coast. Current guidance shows a strengthening subtropical jet off the coast of the Mid-Atlantic, with an associated tight thermal gradient south and east of southern New England. As expected, models show 850-700mb frontogenesis maximized in this thermal gradient along and south of southern New England. These factors do not bode confidence in this system bringing large scale impacts to Vermont, but raw guidance including statistical and AI- driven forecast suggest it is worth continuing to monitor. We recently highlighted preparedness for winter weather across New England, and so it is good to be ready whether or not something takes place. NBC5 METEOROLOGIST (2026-11-09T17:49:00Z — same caveat): Cloudy and cool, few lingering showers Monday afternoon — Monday afternoon will be mostly cloudy and seasonably cool, with a few leftover light showers. Additional summit snowflakes are possible. Highs reach the upper 40s and low 50s, with a stiff northwest breeze. Tonight turns drier, with only a lingering sprinkle or flurry. Expect a mostly cloudy sky, with lows in the 30s to around 40. After a dry start to Tuesday, another round of scattered showers comes through by afternoon and evening. Northern areas will be cloudy, with highs near 50. Southern Vermont likely manages more breaks of sun. Some towns see highs near 60. Wednesday (Veterans Day) looks mostly dry, with only a spot shower or flurry possible. However, it will be mostly cloudy and chilly, with highs in the upper 40s. The late-week stretch looks quite chilly, as the jet stream dips farther south. Highs only reach the low to mid-40s, with lots of clouds. A mix of rain and elevation snow showers are likely Thursday, especially by afternoon. A period of steadier rain and elevation snow is possible Friday, with showers lingering into the weekend. But, uncertainty remains with how close the storm system tracks.
